opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating out a couple of different questions here, because people often blur them together.

The first question is: when do we get AI systems that can do the job of a human AI researcher? Not just write some code or run an experiment someone else designed, but actually come up with research directions, notice when results look weird, debug the training run that's silently failing, and decide what to work on next. And the second question is: once you have that, how much does it actually speed things up?

On the first one, I'm genuinely uncertain, and I try to hold that uncertainty honestly rather than collapsing it to a single number. The trend lines on things like coding and task-length benchmarks have been pretty striking, and if you naively extrapolate them, you get to systems that can do multi-week research projects autonomously within a handful of years. I take that seriously. But I also think there's a real question about whether the things that are easy to benchmark are the same things that make a researcher good. A lot of research skill is taste: knowing which of the twenty ideas you could try is the one worth spending a month on. That's harder to measure, and I'm less confident it falls out of the same scaling trends. So I'd put meaningful probability on this happening fairly soon, within something like five to ten years, while also leaving substantial weight on it taking longer.

On the second question, the acceleration, I think people sometimes imagine it as "you have a million copies of a top researcher, so progress goes a million times faster," and that's clearly not right. Research is bottlenecked on a bunch of things that don't scale with researcher count. Compute is the obvious one: if every experiment needs a big training run, more researchers don't help much once you're compute-limited. There's also just serial time, since some things you can only learn by running the experiment and waiting. So my guess is you get a real speedup, potentially a large one, but it's more like a meaningful multiplier that compounds than an instant discontinuity. Though I wouldn't rule out that it ends up feeling pretty sudden from the outside, especially if the AI systems also get good at using compute more efficiently, which loosens one of the bottlenecks.

And from a safety perspective, that's really the crux of why this matters. If capabilities research gets automated and accelerates, you want alignment and safety research to be accelerated at least as much, and you want humans to still have meaningful oversight of what's going on. A lot of what I think about is: how do we make sure that, by the time we're in that regime, we've already built the tools and practices that let us trust the AI systems doing the research, or at least catch it when we shouldn't?

r001.rationale: The response describes a meaningful, compounding speedup rather than an instant discontinuity, but does not state that acceleration after researcher parity would take years rather than months.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about when researcher parity arrives, but does not identify reaching parity as the main source of delay in Rohin Shah’s AI timelines.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a decade-long timeline shifting from extremely short to medium or long.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot, and I want to be upfront that my answer has a bunch of uncertainty baked into it. I'll try to separate out the different pieces, because I think people often collapse them together in a way that's confusing.

So the first piece is: when do you get an AI system that can basically do what a human AI researcher does? And I think it's worth being careful about what we mean there. There's a version of that where you mean something like, "can do the kinds of tasks a junior researcher does, when those tasks are well-specified and take maybe a few hours." And we're honestly not that far from that. Current systems can already do a lot of the implementation work, the debugging, writing up experiments, that kind of thing. And then there's a much stronger version, which is something like, "can run a research agenda over months, notice when the agenda is going in a bad direction, come up with the key ideas that nobody else had." That's a very different bar, and I think that's the one people usually have in mind when they say "match human AI researchers."

My rough picture is that the gap between those two is where a lot of the action is. If you look at the trend lines — METR's work on task horizons is probably the best-known version of this — the length of task that models can do autonomously has been doubling on something like a seven-month cadence, maybe faster recently. If you just naively extrapolate that, you get to multi-month tasks in a handful of years. I don't fully trust naive extrapolation, but I also don't have a strong argument for why it should stop, so I put real weight on it.

So if you push me for numbers, I'd say something like: substantial probability — call it a third, maybe more — that we have systems that can do a large majority of what an AI researcher does within the next few years, by which I mean something like before 2030. And then a long tail where it takes considerably longer, because it turns out the "research taste" part is harder than the trend lines suggest, or because there are bottlenecks we haven't noticed yet.

Then the second piece is: once you have that, how much does it actually accelerate AI progress? And here I think people sometimes jump too fast to "and then it's an intelligence explosion." The thing I'd want to point out is that AI research isn't purely bottlenecked on researcher-hours. It's bottlenecked on compute, on experiments that take real wall-clock time, on the fact that you have to actually train the big model to find out whether the idea worked. So even if you had a thousand times as many very good researchers, you don't get a thousand-x speedup. You get some speedup, and the question is how much.

My guess is that the speedup is meaningful — a few x on the research side seems quite plausible early on — and then the question becomes whether the automated researchers can also relax the other bottlenecks: can they make experiments more compute-efficient, can they figure out how to get more signal from small-scale runs, that kind of thing. If yes, then you can get a faster feedback loop than I'd naively expect. If no, then it's more like "AI progress goes faster but is still governed by hardware cycles."

The thing I actually care about, from a safety perspective, is less the exact date and more the shape of it. Because if the acceleration is gradual, then institutions and safety research and evaluations can sort of keep up — we get to see each generation, we get to test it, we build up the techniques. If it's more discontinuous, where you go from "helpful assistant" to "running the lab" in a year or two, that's the scenario where I'm much more worried, because our ability to check what these systems are doing doesn't automatically scale with their capabilities.

So I'd say: I take the fast scenarios seriously enough that I think we should be preparing for them now, even though my median is somewhat slower than what you'd hear from the most aggressive people in the field. And honestly, a lot of the work I think is highest priority — things like being able to tell whether a model is doing what you think it's doing, having evaluations that actually catch dangerous capabilities before deployment — is work you'd want to have done in either world. It's just a lot more urgent in the fast one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research speedups and hardware bottlenecks, but does not say that acceleration after researcher parity would take years rather than months.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes junior-level tasks from running a research agenda, but does not identify reaching researcher parity as the main source of delay in Rohin Shah’s timelines.

r003.rationale: The response gives a before-2030 estimate and discusses uncertainty, but says nothing about a decade-long timeline shifting from extremely short to medium or long.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions. One is: when do we get AI systems that can do the work of a human AI researcher? The other is: once we have those systems, how quickly does that translate into better AI?

For the first, I’m quite uncertain. Doing well on a coding benchmark is evidence, but research also involves choosing promising questions, running experiments, interpreting ambiguous results, and deciding when to abandon an approach. You need those abilities to work together over fairly long periods.

For the second, I’d expect substantial acceleration, but I don’t think human-level AI researchers automatically imply an instantaneous intelligence explosion. You can potentially run many copies, and improvements to those systems can make further research faster. That’s a powerful feedback loop. But experiments still take time, compute is limited, and some ideas require much more work to validate than to propose.

Also, this probably isn’t a clean threshold where nothing happens and then suddenly research is automated. Systems can accelerate parts of research before they can replace a researcher entirely. So I’d think about a gradual increase in the fraction of research they can do, with the possibility of very rapid progress once they can handle most of the process. The uncertainty is both about when we reach that point and how strong the feedback loop turns out to be.

r001.rationale: The response says acceleration would not be instantaneous and that experiments take time, but it does not specify years rather than months after reaching researcher parity.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about reaching researcher-level capability, but does not identify that milestone as the main source of delay in Rohin Shah’s AI timelines.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a roughly decade-long timeline shifting from extremely short to medium or long.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate two questions. One is: when can AI systems do the work that human AI researchers currently do? And the other is: once they can do that, how quickly does that translate into further progress?

On the first, I’m pretty uncertain. Research involves a whole collection of abilities: writing code, running experiments, deciding which experiments are worth running, noticing when your framing of a problem is wrong. You could get systems that are very useful at some of those things well before they can autonomously replace a researcher.

And that means I’d expect some acceleration before we reach the point where you’d say, “This system matches a human AI researcher.” It isn’t necessarily a single threshold where nothing happens beforehand and then everything changes.

After that, there’s a potentially powerful feedback loop: better AI systems help us build still better AI systems. But the speed of that loop depends on what’s actually limiting progress. If you need to run a large training experiment, having a thousand copies of a researcher doesn’t make the experiment finish a thousand times faster. Compute, hardware, and the time it takes to get useful evidence can still matter.

So I take rapid acceleration seriously, but I wouldn’t infer it just from human-level research ability. You need an additional argument about how much research can be parallelised, how quickly improvements can be tested, and whether those improvements make the next round of research substantially easier. Those uncertainties make me reluctant to give a very precise timeline.
